parsed.explanation: The inductive step invokes the IH on $(\mathcal F_c, C\setminus\{c\})$ as a FULL classification ('a finite set meets every member of $\mathcal F_c$ iff it contains some $D_{c,k}$'), then infers 'a transversal $X$ meeting $C$ … traverses $\mathcal F_c$, so it contains a corresponding $D_{c,k}$.' But the step proves only the restricted assertion ('we only need to restrict attention to transversals meeting $C$'). At recursive levels $C\setminus\{c\}$ need not belong to $\mathcal F_c$, so transversals of $\mathcal F_c$ disjoint from it exist and are unclassified. Concrete witness: $\mathcal F=\{\{1,2\},\{1,3\},\{2,3\}\}$, $C=\{1,2\}\in\mathcal F$, $X=\{1,3\}$: $\mathcal F_1=\{\{2,3\}\}$, $C\setminus\{1\}=\{2\}\notin\mathcal F_1$, and $X$ traverses $\mathcal F_1$ while missing $\{2\}$; no restricted list forces a $D_{1,k}\subseteq X$. The 'inherited from a member' remark supplies no repair. The whole finiteness/periodicity argument rests solely on this lemma, so the proof is invalid as written (though the lemma itself is true).
